card: Paper card. Question: How can the strength–ductility synergy in eutectic high-entropy alloys be improved by inheriting the composite lamellar nature through tailored thermo-mechanical processing?. System: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 (at%) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA). Processing: Arc-melting followed by suction-casting into a copper mold, multi-pass cold-rolling to 84–86% reduction in thickness, and non-isothermal annealing at 660, 700, 740, or 900 °C for 1 h with a heating rate of 10 °C min−1 followed by water quenching.. Test conditions: Room temperature tensile tests with an initial strain rate of 2.5 × 10−4 s−1 using dog-bone specimens (15 mm gauge length, 3.2 mm width, 600 μm thickness) and loading–unloading–reloading (LUR) tests.. Findings: The DPHL700 and DPHL740 samples achieved a yield strength of approximately 1.5 GPa with an elongation of ~16%, representing a simultaneous enhancement in both strength and ductility compared to as-cast and ultrafine-grained counterparts.; The microstructure exhibited a two-hierarchical heterogeneity consisting of submicron-grade FCC/B2 grains within FCC lamellae and micron-grade alternate FCC/B2 lamellae.; The average diameters of FCC and B2 grains were roughly comparable at ~0.71 μm, with inter-lamella spacings ranging from 1.5 to 5 μm.; Phase decomposition resulted in two types of NiAl-rich precipitates in FCC lamellae: small intragranular P1 grains (50–180 nm) and large intergranular P2 grains (~350 nm).; Back-stress measurements at the yield point reached ~950 MPa, which was approximately 3 times higher than the effective stress, primarily responsible for the high yield strength.; The strain-hardening rate (Θ) showed a transient behavior with an up-turn in region II and sustained high Θ over a wide strain region III for DPHL700.; Microcrack-arresting mechanisms were observed where multiple microcracks were inhibited from coalescing, with ductile components acting as efficient crack arresters.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the enhanced properties to a two-hierarchical constraint effect that generates long-range back-stress by storing geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs) due to strain gradients at lamella interfaces and around intergranular precipitates, combined with a self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanism where the aligned lamellar architecture delays crack propagation and coalescence.. Limitations: The authors note that while the DPHL structure is effective, increasing the annealing temperature to 900 °C induced a partially degraded lamellar structure that led to inferior tensile properties, indicating the sensitivity of the process to thermal treatment.. Future work: The authors propose that further efforts should be devoted to exploring non-equiatomic alloys and spinodal decomposition to create low-misfit coherent nanostructures for even higher yield strengths, and anticipate modifying the EHEA to satisfy requirements for high-temperature and/or corrosion environments.. Quote: "The as-prepared samples exhibit hierarchically-structural heterogeneity due to phase decomposition, and the improved mechanical response during deformation is attributed to both a two-hierarchical constraint effect and a self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanism."

W2622849719.title: Phase‐Transformation Ductilization of Brittle High‐Entropy Alloys via Metastability Engineering

card: Paper card. Question: How can high-entropy alloys be designed to achieve ultra-high strength while retaining good ductility, overcoming the limitation of near-equiatomic compositions that restrict the formation of high-volume fractions of ductile strengthening precipitates?. System: Al0.5Cr0.9FeNi2.5V0.2 (non-equiatomic, ~50 at% Ni, ~18 at% Cr, ~4 at% V). Processing: Arc-melting pure metals, casting into copper mold, solution-treating at 1200 °C for 24 h followed by water quenching, cold-rolling with 72% reduction ratio, and ageing at 600 °C or 700 °C for 1 h followed by air cooling.. Test conditions: Room temperature tensile testing with a nominal strain rate of 1 × 10−3 s−1 on dog-bone-shaped samples (gauge length 10 mm, width 3 mm, thickness 1 mm).. Findings: Achieved an ultrahigh yield strength of 1810 MPa and ultimate tensile strength of 1905 MPa in the sample aged at 600 °C.; The strength increment relative to the solution-treated sample was >1500 MPa (>560%).; Retained good ductility with elongation of ~9–10% after achieving the maximum strength.; Formed high-content ordered L12 nanoprecipitates with a volume fraction of ~50.1% in the 600 A sample.; The L12 phases are coherent with the FCC matrix, with a lattice parameter difference of only 0.0001 nm (0.3582 nm vs 0.3583 nm).; The spinodal nanostructure contributed 1158 MPa to the yield strength, while grain boundaries contributed 212 MPa.; The total estimated yield strength increase (1524 MPa) agrees closely with the experimental result (1536 MPa).; The mean diameter of the ordered L12 precipitates was determined to be ~35 nm.. Mechanism: The alloying strategy utilizes spinodal decomposition to create a low-misfit coherent nanostructure where the L12 nanophases resist dislocation motion by providing strong diffuse attractive obstacles to trap moving dislocations and by creating antiphase boundaries (APBs) on the slip planes when sheared by dislocations. The diffuse coherent interfaces minimize elastic strain accumulation, preventing crack initiation and maintaining ductility.. Limitations: The authors note that the calculated strengthening contributions based on assuming spherical precipitates may underestimate the area of APBs and the strengthening effect because the actual L12 phases are irregular and interconnected. Additionally, the volume fraction calculations may not be absolutely precise.. Future work: The authors anticipate that this alloying strategy can offer more possibilities for the compositional design of HEAs and will open new avenues for development of ultrastrong and ductile HEAs superior to existing commercial alloys, potentially competing with traditional structural materials in rigorous service conditions.. Quote: "Here we present a strategy to design ultrastrong HEAs with high-content nanoprecipitates by phase separation, which can generate a near-equiatomic matrix in situ while forming strengthening phases"

W2893800769.title: High-content ductile coherent nanoprecipitates achieve ultrastrong high-entropy alloys

card: Paper card. Question: How can a single-phase face-centered cubic medium-entropy alloy achieve both gigapascal yield strength and high uniform ductility without relying on second-phase heterogeneities?. System: Equimolar CrCoNi medium-entropy alloy (33.48Cr-32.46Co-34.06Ni atomic percent). Processing: Electromagnetic levitation melting, homogenization at 1,473 K for 12 h, hot forging (1,323–1,173 K), cold rolling to 0.5 mm sheets, followed by partial recrystallization annealing at 873 K for 1 h and water quenching. Test conditions: Quasi-static uniaxial tensile tests at strain rate 5 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹, room temperature (298 K) and liquid nitrogen temperature (77 K); loading-unloading-reloading (LUR) tests to measure back stresses. Findings: Yield strength (σ0.2) of ~1,150 MPa achieved with a three-level heterogeneous grain structure (HGS) spanning nanometer to micrometer scales.; Uniform tensile strain (Eu) reached 22% at room temperature, significantly higher than the ~2% Eu observed in homogeneous ultrafine-grained counterparts with similar strength.; The number density of nanograins (ρNG) increased from 4.7 grains/µm² before testing to 21 grains/µm² after deformation at 298 K and 31 grains/µm² at 77 K.; Back stress hardening accounted for over 80% of the total stress elevation observed during strain hardening from yield to ultimate tensile stress.; The strain hardening rate (Θ) exhibited a distinct upturn between 4% and 8% strain, contrasting with the monotonic drop seen in homogeneous structures.; The width of hysteresis loops in LUR tests was the largest ever recorded for any known alloy, indicating exceptionally high internal back stresses.; Corner twins evolved into nanograins during tensile straining, dynamically reinforcing the heterogeneity of the grain structure.. Mechanism: The heterogeneous grain structure induces load partitioning and strain gradient hardening, causing dislocation pile-ups at grain boundaries and generating geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs). This creates large long-range internal back stresses that sustain strain hardening. Additionally, the low stacking fault energy facilitates the dynamic generation of twinned nanograins at grain boundaries during deformation, which further refines the structure and perpetuates back stress hardening.. Limitations: The beneficial effects of the HGS diminish if the material undergoes extended annealing toward uniform grains or if the alloy has high stacking fault energy where full dislocations dominate and recover/annihilate easily.. Future work: The authors propose that this strategy is generally applicable to other single-phase low-SFE alloys and metals to achieve simultaneous high yield strength and high tensile ductility.. Quote: "This heterogeneity results from this alloy's low stacking fault energy, which facilitates corner twins in recrystallization and stores deformation twins and stacking faults during tensile straining."

W2302110147.title: Strain hardening in Fe–16Mn–10Al–0.86C–5Ni high specific strength steel

card: Paper card. Question: How can cryo-rolling and annealing be utilized to overcome the strength-ductility trade-off in multiphase high entropy alloys, specifically regarding the development of a hierarchical microstructure?. System: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high entropy alloy (EHEA). Processing: Multi-pass cryo-rolling up to ~90% reduction in thickness with immersion in liquid N2 for 45 minutes before and after each pass, followed by annealing at 800 °C for 1 hour and water quenching.. Test conditions: Tensile tests at ambient temperature with an initial strain rate of 8.3 × 10−4 s−1; Nano-indentation with load increased linearly from 1 μN to 500 μN over 0.25 seconds.. Findings: The cryo-rolled and annealed material achieved a Yield Strength (YS) of 1437 ± 26 MPa and Ultimate Tensile Strength (UTS) of 1562 ± 33 MPa.; The elongation to failure (ef) was approximately 14 ± 1%, which remained almost unchanged compared to the as-cast material (17 ± 1%).; The hierarchical microstructure consists of fine lamellar regions with ultrafine FCC grains (average size ~200–250 nm) and coarse non-lamellar regions with coarse unrecrystallized B2 phase (~2.5 µm).; The hardness of the B2 phase (~12 GPa) is nearly three times higher than that of the L12 phase (~4 GPa) in the as-cast material.; The cryo-rolled and annealed material covers the entire hardness spectrum with softer regions (≤8 GPa), intermediate regions (~8–12 GPa), and much harder regions (≥12 GPa).; The cold-rolled and annealed material showed a homogenous microduplex morphology with grain sizes of ~0.5 µm, unlike the heterogeneous cryo-rolled structure.; The cryo-rolled and annealed EHEA possesses the highest YS and UTS while maintaining appreciable ductility compared to other HEAs like Al0.5CoCrCuFeNi and Fe40Mn27Ni26Co5Cr2.. Mechanism: The simultaneous enhancement in strength and ductility originates from a characteristic hierarchical microstructure that creates profuse domain boundaries separating domains of different hardness, leading to significant back stress strengthening and delayed necking due to strain gradients and geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs).. Limitations: The text does not explicitly state limitations of the study.. Future work: The text does not explicitly state future work.. Quote: "The hierarchical microstructure of the cryo-rolled and annealed material resulted in simultaneous enhancement in strength (Yield Strength/YS: 1437 ± 26 MPa, Ultimate Tensile Strength/UTS: 1562 ± 33 MPa) and ductility (elongation to failure/ef ~ 14 ± 1%)"

card: Paper card. Question: How can the strength of twinning-induced plasticity (TWIP) steel be enhanced without sacrificing ductility, thereby evading the long-standing strength–ductility trade-off dilemma?. System: FeMnC TWIP steel (23.84% Mn, 0.61% C, balanced Fe) with a low stacking fault energy of 15–30 m Jm−2. Processing: Cylindrical samples were subjected to torsion (180° or 360°) at an angular loading rate of 0.05° s−1 to generate a gradient nanotwinned structure, followed by uniaxial tensile deformation at a strain rate of ~10−4 s−1. Test conditions: Torsion tests at 0.05° s−1; tensile tests at ~10−4 s−1; micro-hardness measured with 500 g load for 15 s; microstructure analyzed via SEM, EBSD, and TEM (200 kV). Findings: Yielding strength of the pre-torsioned TWIP steel was doubled to ~730 MPa (from ~300 MPa) with no reduction in ductility.; A gradient nanotwinned structure formed with twin density increasing from the center to the outermost region (r/R=1).; Twin thickness increased with radial distance, reaching tens of nanometers at the surface.; Subsequent tensile deformation activated secondary and tertiary twins, creating a hierarchical nanotwinned structure.; The hardening modulus remained high until sample failure, unlike traditional processing which reduces ductility.; Finite element simulations showed yielding strength follows a law of mixture, with the hard shell significantly raising the yield strength of the soft core.; Different twinning systems were activated during torsion (e.g., T2, T4) compared to subsequent tension (e.g., T5, T1).; Dislocation dissociation at twin boundaries avoided stress concentration, playing a crucial role in retaining ductility.. Mechanism: The gradient hierarchical nanotwinned structure enhances strength through the hard shell/soft core effect and twin barriers, while ductility is retained because sequential torsion and tension activate different twinning systems, creating a 3D hierarchical network that distributes plasticity and prevents premature failure via localized necking.. Limitations: The method relies on materials prone to deformation twinning (low stacking fault energy); applying the same pre-torsion to 6061 Aluminum alloy resulted in enhanced strength but reduced ductility due to the lack of a hierarchical nanotwin network.. Future work: Develop other methods to produce non-uniform shear strains in metals prone to deformation twinning to enhance material performance, potentially applicable to axially symmetric structural components like axles in machines and high-speed trains.. Quote: "we find that the yielding strength of the material can be doubled at no reduction in ductility."

card: Paper card. Question: Can nanodomained nickel unite nanocrystal strength with coarse-grain ductility?. System: Nickel (Ni) with nanoscale domains. Processing: Pulsed electrodeposition with a grain refiner. Test conditions: Quasi-static uniaxial tensile tests at a strain rate of 5 × 10−4 s−1 at room temperature. Findings: The nanodomained Ni achieves a yield strength approaching 1.3 GPa; The material exhibits a uniform elongation as large as ~30%; The nanoscale domains effectively block dislocations and provide dislocation sources and trapping sites; The nanodomains occupy only ~2.4% of the total volume; The average domain diameter is ~7 nm. Mechanism: The nanoscale domains act as strong obstacles to dislocation movements, and their boundaries provide dislocation sources and trapping sites, leading to enhanced strain hardening. Limitations: The stability of the nanodomains during long-time sample storage and deformation is not fully understood. Future work: Further research is needed to explore the potential of this strategy for other metals and alloys. Quote: "the nanodomains would elevate the strength to GPa level"

card: Paper card. Question: Can friction stir processing (FSP) enhance the strength and ductility of a dual-phase high-entropy alloy (HEA) with a composition of Fe50Mn30Co10Cr10 (at.%)?. System: Fe50Mn30Co10Cr10 (at.%) dual-phase high-entropy alloy. Processing: Friction stir processing (FSP) with tool rotational rates of 350 and 650 RPM. Test conditions: Tensile testing at room temperature with an initial strain rate of 10−3 s−1. Findings: The FSP-engineered microstructure exhibited a substantially smaller grain size, with average grain sizes of 6.5 and 5.2 µm, respectively.; The FSP treatment led to a significantly higher fraction of f.c.c. γ-phase in the microstructure of the TRIP HEA.; The FSP specimens showed enhanced strength and ductility, with maximum true stress values of 1400 MPa and 1200 MPa at uniform elongations of almost 45% and 42%, respectively.; The TRIP effect was enhanced in the FSP specimens, with a higher level of TRIP-related strain hardening during deformation.; The strength-ductility index (SDI) values of the FSP specimens were higher than those of the as-homogenized reference material.; The FSP-engineered DP-HEA showed a similar f.c.c. γ average grain size as compared to the TMP-HEA reported by Li et al., but with a lower h.c.p. ε-phase fraction.; The difference in the SDI values for the 350 and 650 RPM treated specimens could be explained by considering both the grain refinement and the ε-phase fraction prior to tensile deformation.. Mechanism: The enhanced strength and ductility of the FSP-engineered HEA were attributed to the synergistic effects of grain boundary strengthening, TRIP, and effective strain partitioning between the γ and ε phases during deformation.. Limitations: The study only investigated the effects of FSP on the microstructure and mechanical properties of the HEA, without exploring other processing techniques or conditions.. Future work: Further studies are needed to optimize the processing conditions and explore the potential of FSP for other HEA compositions.. Quote: "Friction stir processing resulted in a fine grain size along with a high volume fraction of f.c.c. (γ) phase as compared to as-homogenized reference material."

card: Paper card. Question: How can nanoprecipitates be designed and controlled in high-entropy alloys (HEAs) to achieve high strength while maintaining good ductility, and what are the specific mechanisms governing their formation and strengthening effects?. System: FCC-based HEAs including (FeCoNiCr)94Ti2Al4, Ni2CoCrFeNb0.15, Al0.3Cu0.5CrFeNi2, CoCrFeNi(Ni3Al)x, and (Ni1.5FeCoCr0.5)87.5Al7.5Ti5.0; also BCC-based systems like AlxCoCrCuFeNi and refractory systems like TaNbHfZrTi. Processing: Aging heat treatments at temperatures ranging from 550 °C to 1000 °C for durations from 150 h to 720 h; severe plastic deformation for grain refinement; mechanical alloying (MA) for high-density particle introduction; laser cladding for coatings; and direct addition of stoichiometric strengthening phases (e.g., Ni3Al) to the matrix. Test conditions: Room temperature tensile testing; compression testing; corrosion testing in NaCl and sulfuric acid solutions; hardness measurements (HV); microstructural analysis via TEM/SEM after aging; cryogenic treatment at -40 °C. Findings: The Ni2CoCrFeNb0.15 HEA aged at 650 °C for 80 h retained D022-Ni3Nb precipitates with a size of only ≈15 nm, demonstrating the slow diffusion effect in HEAs.; The (FeCoNiCr)94Ti2Al4 HEA achieved a yield strength of ≈1005 MPa and tensile strength of ≈1,273 MPa with an elongation of ≈17% due to nanoprecipitate strengthening.; In the Al0.3Cu0.5CrFeNi2 HEA, adding 0.073 at% C promoted M23C6 carbide formation, increasing yield strength by 193 MPa and ultimate tensile strength by 415 MPa while maintaining 88% elongation.; The (Ni1.5FeCoCr0.5)87.5Al7.5Ti5.0 HEA exhibited a yield strength >1.0 GPa, tensile strength ≈1.5 GPa, and elongation ≈50% due to a unique nanolamellar structure with coherent boundaries.; The Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA aged at 800 °C showed a precipitate size increase of only 6 nm (from 45 nm to 51 nm) between 50 h and 100 h aging, indicating slow coarsening.; In the CoCrFeNiMo0.3 alloy, the precipitation of fine σ and μ intermetallic phases resulted in a yield strength of 816 MPa, tensile strength of 1.2 GPa, and elongation of 19%.; The γ′ phase in HEAs can be stabilized by adjusting the Ti/Al ratio; a ratio within 0.7–2 favors L12 phase formation, while Ti/Al = 1/3 favors B2 phase formation.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the superior performance to the 'slow diffusion' effect in HEAs, which limits precipitate growth and coarsening, allowing for the retention of fine nanoscale precipitates. Strengthening mechanisms include Orowan bypass for incoherent large precipitates, dislocation cutting for coherent nanoscale precipitates (L12, D022), order strengthening due to atomic arrangement, and grain refinement strengthening where carbides suppress grain growth. The 'cocktail effect' and high mixing entropy also contribute to phase stability and the formation of simple solid solutions.. Limitations: The text states that the influence of the size and type of nanoprecipitates on the strengthening effect is still not clear, and the design method and precipitation conditions are relatively vague. Additionally, increasing the volume fraction of γ′ precipitates can increase the risk of forming harmful intermetallic compounds or cause processing problems. Over-aging can lead to the transformation of metastable phases into hard, brittle intermetallic compounds (like δ, σ, or η phases), which deteriorate mechanical properties.. Future work: The authors outline the need to further explore the effects of the types and sizes of nanoprecipitates on the strengthening effect. They propose using the OVEC (valence electron concentration) design strategy to control precipitate structures. Future work should focus on alloy-design strategies that consider the matrix composition after precipitates separate out, rather than just the initial composition, to maintain the advantages of HEAs.. Quote: "The characteristics of multiple principal elements and slow diffusion effect of elements in HEAs provide a chance to form fine and stable nanoscale precipitates, pushing the strengths of the alloys to new high levels."

Paper card. Question: How can new nanoprecipitates and strengthening mechanisms be designed to achieve high strength without sacrificing ductility in high-entropy alloys, and what are the specific characteristics required for these precipitates and their matrix?. System: Fe25Co25Ni25Al10Ti15 (FCC matrix with L12 γ' and γ* phases), Al0.7CoCrFeNi (B2 phase with Cr-rich BCC precipitates), Al0.2CrFeCoNi2Cu0.2, lightweight Al1.5CrFeMnTi (BCC matrix with L21 phase), and refractory (TiZrHfNb)98O2. Processing: Aging treatments at temperatures between 600 and 800 °C; specific examples include aging at 700 °C for 20 h or 800 °C for 1 h; solution aging followed by direct aging; annealing to change size, shape, and coherency of L21 phases; addition of 2.0 at% O to TaNbHfZrTi. Test conditions: Aging temperatures ranging from 550 to 800 °C; aging times of 1 h to 20 h; tensile testing at room temperature (yield strength 1.11 ± 0.03 GPa, ductility 27.66% ± 1.13%); diffusion couple experiments at 1273–1373 K. Findings: The Fe25Co25Ni25Al10Ti15 HEA with Ω = 1.119 and δ = 6.277 generated a γ′ phase with an L12 structure in a disordered FCC matrix.; In dual-phase FCC + B2 structures, ellipsoidal-ordered L12 precipitates with a diameter of 8 nm were observed in FCC dendrites, while BCC-structured precipitates with a diameter around 10 nm were observed in B2 dendrites.; The precipitation temperature of γ′ nano-precipitates is between 600 and 800 °C, which is higher than that of other γ′ phases (500–750 °C).; In Al0.2CrFeCoNi2Cu0.2, the L12 phase was present after aging at 700 °C for 20 h, but no nanoscale precipitation occurred after 1 h at 800 °C.; Re-precipitation of the Laves phase was detected inside grains and on grain boundaries in solution-aging samples, whereas direct-aging samples only contained γ and γ′ phases.; The tensile yield strength of the (TiZrHfNb)98O2 refractory HEA reached 1.11 ± 0.03 GPa with a tensile ductility of 27.66% ± 1.13%.; Cu-rich nanoprecipitates precipitate around 700 °C with slower kinetics compared to the L12-ordered phase.; Carbides exhibit a much wider precipitation temperature range (550–800 °C) and are more stable than other precipitates.. Mechanism: Small lattice mismatch between nanoprecipitates and the matrix reduces specific interface energy, stabilizing nanoscale size; high shear modulus and antiphase-domain-boundary energy hinder dislocation cutting, providing coherent, modulus, and ordered strengthening; high number density is achieved via low driving force of nucleation and matrix defects; twin boundaries and phase-transformation-induced plasticity absorb dislocations to improve plasticity; nanoprecipitates act as traps for irradiation-induced vacancies and interstitials.. Limitations: Comprehensive mechanical properties do not yet reach full potentials; almost all effective nanoprecipitates are derived from superalloys with no unique HEA-specific precipitates found; negative effects include nanoprecipitate coarsening or crystal-structure transformation during high-temperature service; matrix phase design for functional properties often fails to meet expected comprehensive mechanical properties simultaneously.. Future work: Explore new nanoprecipitates and strengthening mechanisms that enhance strength without sacrificing ductility; investigate the slow diffusion effect in HEAs to better understand nucleation and growth of precipitates; study the interactions between intrinsic heterogeneities and precipitates; introduce nanoprecipitates into lightweight, refractory, and radiation-resistant HEA systems; utilize high-density dislocations and modulated FCC-to-BCC transformations for strengthening.. Quote: "The new type of nanoprecipitates should exhibit a strength enhancement without scarifying the ductility."

card: Paper card. Question: Can a hierarchical architecture involving secondary nanoprecipitates form inside primary nanoprecipitates in high-entropy alloys, and can an ultrahigh strength be achieved through a high density of such intragranular hierarchical nanoprecipitates?. System: Fe25Co25Ni25Al10Ti15 (atomic %). Processing: Mechanical alloying (MA) for 49 hours (45h dry + 4h wet with ethanol) followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS) at 1000°C, 30 MPa pressure, 90°C/min heating rate, and <8 Pa vacuum.. Test conditions: Room temperature uniaxial tension using in situ SEM microtensile testing with a nominal strain rate of 1 × 10−3 s−1; in situ TEM compression tests at room temperature with an axial displacement rate of 3 nm s–1.. Findings: Tensile yield strength (σ0.2) of ~1.86 GPa and ultimate tensile strength of ~2.52 GPa at room temperature.; Failure strain of ~5.2% achieved alongside the ultrahigh strength values.; Microstructure consists of a primary fcc phase (~82.3 vol %) and a small amount of bcc phase (~17.7 vol %).; The fcc matrix contains a high density of hierarchical intragranular nanoprecipitates: primary γ′ (L12 structure, ~57 nm avg diameter, ~62 vol % in fcc) and secondary γ* (A1 structure, several nm to tens of nm).; Average spacing between adjacent γ′ nanoprecipitates is ~11 nm.; Dislocations were observed to shear both the primary γ′ and secondary γ* precipitates during in situ TEM compression.; Grain diameters average ~409 nm for the fcc phase and ~227 nm for the bcc phase.. Mechanism: The ultrahigh strength is primarily attributed to precipitation strengthening via the shearing mechanism, where dislocations shear both the primary coherent γ′ precipitates and the secondary coherent γ* precipitates, creating an 'exaggerated precipitation strengthening effect' due to the hierarchical obstacle distribution. Additional contributions come from grain-boundary strengthening (due to submicrometer grains) and load transfer via the hard bcc phase.. Limitations: The chemical composition of the secondary γ* precipitates could not be obtained due to their very small sizes.. Future work: The authors suggest the design strategy provides insight for achieving ultrahigh strength in HEAs or other multicomponent alloys, implying further exploration of hierarchical architectures, though specific future experiments are not explicitly detailed beyond the general validation of the strategy.. Quote: "Here, we report a strategy for the design and fabrication of HEAs that can achieve ultrahigh tensile strengths."

card: Paper card. Question: How does the precipitation of ordered L12 intermetallics within the fcc phase of a eutectic Al0.7CoCrFeNi high entropy alloy influence its strain-rate dependent mechanical behavior, specifically yield strength, work hardening, and deformation mechanisms under quasi-static versus dynamic loading?. System: Al0.7CoCrFeNi (15 at.% Al, 21.25 at.% each of Co, Cr, Fe, Ni) forming a lamellar dual-phase microstructure of fcc + B2 (with B2 containing bcc nano-precipitates), further modified by L12 precipitation in the fcc phase.. Processing: Melting of elemental constituents, homogenization at 1150 °C for 1 h, cold rolling to 30% reduction, annealing at 1100 °C for 5 mins (CR-H condition), and low-temperature annealing at 580 °C for 24 h (CR-H-580 condition).. Test conditions: Quasi-static tensile loading at a strain rate of 10−3 s−1 and dynamic compressive loading using a split Hopkinson pressure bar (SHPB) at a strain rate of 2 × 103 s−1.. Findings: The CR-H-580 condition with L12 precipitates exhibited a yield strength of ~1080 MPa and UTS of ~1370 MPa under quasi-static loading, compared to ~770 MPa YS and ~1090 MPa UTS for the CR-H condition.; Under dynamic loading (2 × 103 s−1), flow stresses reached ~1800 MPa for the CR-H-580 condition without failure up to 20% strain.; The introduction of L12 precipitates resulted in a precipitation strengthening of ~310 MPa, which compares reasonably well with the Orowan model prediction of ~360 MPa.; The steady-state work hardening rate increased from ~3000 MPa in the CR-H condition to >4000 MPa in the CR-H-580 condition.; The strain rate sensitivity (SRS) parameter (m) at 1% flow stress was 0.018 for CR-H and 0.017 for CR-H-580, indicating L12 precipitation did not significantly alter SRS.; Post-deformation analysis revealed that the L12 phase disorders under both quasi-static and dynamic deformation, forming anti-phase boundaries.; High density of twins (approx. 20 nm thick) was observed in the fcc phase under dynamic testing, whereas only fine-scale nano-twins were seen under quasi-static testing.; APT analysis showed L12 precipitates have a radius of ~3–5 nm, a volume fraction of ~9.5% within the fcc lamellae, and a composition of ~56.4 at.% Ni and ~35.8 at.% Al.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the strength increase to the Orowan dislocation bowing and bypass mechanism by coherent L12 precipitates. The high work hardening is explained by the capability of the lamellar structure to store high dislocation densities at interfaces and the formation of anti-phase boundaries upon L12 disordering. The lack of significant change in SRS is rationalized by the presence of precipitate-free channels near the lamellar boundaries which act as sites for high dislocation storage, and the thermally activated nature of the coherent L12 precipitates.. Limitations: The text notes that detailed first-principles computational studies are needed to establish the exact site-occupancies of elements within the ordered L12 structure due to the unusually high Al content. It also mentions that the B2 lamellae are not continuous but pinched off at the microscopic scale.. Future work: The authors state that detailed first-principles, electronic structure based computational studies need to be coupled with experimental observations to establish the site-occupancies of different elements within the ordered L12 structure.. Quote: "Low temperature annealing leads to the precipitation of ordered L12 intermetallic precipitates within the fcc resulting in enhanced strength."

card: Paper card. Question: How can a Co-Cr-Ni-based medium-entropy alloy be designed to achieve simultaneous ultra-high strength and sufficient uniform ductility by controlling composition, thermomechanical processing, and microstructural features?. System: Co34.46Cr32.12Ni27.42Al3Ti3 (in at%) medium-entropy alloy with FCC matrix and L12 precipitates. Processing: Vacuum induction melting, homogenization at 1200 °C for 2 h, hot-rolling at 1100 °C (50% reduction), cryo-rolling (CR) at 77 K to 80% total reduction, high-temperature annealing at 900 °C for 1 h (CRA), and subsequent aging at 700 °C for 4 h (CRAA). Test conditions: Uniaxial tensile testing at ambient temperature with a constant strain rate of 1 × 10−3 s−1. Findings: Achieved ultimate tensile strength (σu) of 2.2 GPa and uniform elongation (εue) of 13% in the CRAA-treated alloy.; The dual heterogeneous structure consists of a matrix with coarse grains (10–30 μm) and ultra-fine grains (0.5–2 μm).; Heterogeneous L12 nanoprecipitates range from several to hundreds of nanometers with a total volume fraction of 24.2%.; The lattice mismatch between the FCC matrix and L12 precipitates is extremely low at 0.011%.; The average size of fine L12 precipitates is 4.14 ± 0.62 nm with a number density of 3.4 × 1024 m−3.; Strengthening contributions calculated as: solid-solution (49 MPa), HDI hardening (800 MPa), and precipitation hardening (1115 MPa).; No twins or hexagonal close-packed (HCP) phase formed after deformation up to ~2.0 GPa stress.; Dislocation density in the fractured sample reached 3.83 × 1014 m−2 due to Lomer–Cottrell locks.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the superior properties to a combination of HDI strengthening from the heterogeneous grain structure, precipitation hardening from high-density coherent L12 particles, and enhanced ductility from the low elastic misfit strain of the interfaces which relieves stress concentration and prevents premature fracture, while the preservation of stacking faults and high dislocation density provides significant work-hardening.. Limitations: The text does not explicitly state limitations of the study.. Future work: The authors state that the strategy opens a new avenue for the development of promising heavy-duty structural materials and that the alloy elements and treatments can be readily accepted by industry.. Quote: "a Co-Cr-Ni-based medium-entropy alloy (MEA) with a dual heterogeneous structure of both matrix and precipitates can be designed to provide an ultra-high tensile strength of 2.2 GPa and uniform elongation of 13%"

card: Paper card. Question: How can severe cryo-rolling followed by annealing be used to tailor heterogeneous microstructures and overcome the strength-ductility trade-off in brittle intermetallic-containing high entropy alloys?. System: CoCrFeNi2.1Nb0.2 high entropy alloy (FCC matrix with complex Laves phase particles). Processing: Homogenized ingots (1200 °C/24 h) were multi-pass cold- or cryo-rolled to 90% reduction in thickness (final thickness ~0.4 mm); cryo-rolling involved immersion in liquid N2 for 0.5 h before and after every pass; subsequent annealing at 800 °C for 1 h followed by water quenching.. Test conditions: Tensile tests conducted at ambient temperature with an initial strain rate of 1 × 10−3 s−1 using dog-bone shaped specimens.. Findings: Cryo-rolling resulted in a finer lamellar nanostructure with an average HAB spacing of ~50 ± 9 nm compared to ~65 ± 12 nm in cold-rolled samples.; The Laves phase particles showed greater fragmentation in cryo-rolled samples (average size ~0.68 ± 0.40 µm) compared to cold-rolled samples (~1.00 ± 0.44 µm).; The cryo-rolled and annealed HEA achieved a yield strength of 1219 ± 14 MPa and ultimate tensile strength of 1272 ± 25 MPa with ~22% elongation.; The cold-rolled and annealed HEA showed a yield strength of 774 ± 13 MPa and ultimate tensile strength of 1085 ± 18 MPa with ~20% elongation.; The yield strength of the cryo-rolled and annealed HEA was increased by ~400 MPa (~58% increase) compared to the cold-rolled and annealed HEA.; The cryo-rolled and annealed HEA exhibited a heterogeneous microstructure with co-existing deformed and recrystallized regions, whereas the cold-rolled HEA was predominantly recrystallized.; Profuse ε nano-precipitates formed early in the cryo-rolled HEA (after 120 s at 800 °C), inhibiting recrystallization via Zener pinning, while precipitation lagged recrystallization in the cold-rolled HEA.. Mechanism: The heterogeneous microstructure originates from accelerated precipitation of the nanosized ε phase early in the recrystallization process due to a greater density of nucleation sites (dislocations, shear bands, grain boundaries) in the cryo-rolled HEA; these precipitates pin high-angle boundaries (Zener pinning), inhibiting recrystallization and creating a mix of deformed and recrystallized regions; mechanical incompatibility between these domains generates strain gradients and geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs), creating long-range back stress that delays necking and enhances both strength and ductility.. Limitations: The back stress generated by the heterogeneous microstructure was not quantified in this study.. Future work: The authors suggest that the results indicate significant opportunities for achieving novel heterogeneous microstructures in a wide range of HEAs through innovative processing by cryo-rolling.. Quote: "Cryo-rolling resulted in a finer lamellar nanostructure and decidedly greater fragmentation of the Laves phase."

card: Paper card. Question: Can shear band-driven precipitate dispersion be used to create ultrastrong ductile medium-entropy alloys?. System: Al0.2CoNiV medium-entropy alloy. Processing: Cold-rolling and subsequent heat treatment at 800, 850, and 900 °C for 1 h. Test conditions: Room-temperature tensile tests. Findings: The A800 alloy exhibits a yield strength of 1500 MPa and an ultimate tensile strength of 1727 MPa; The A850 alloy shows a remarkable strength-ductility balance of 1587 MPa × 26.7%; The L21 precipitates have a semicoherent interface with the disordered FCC matrix; The micro-shear bands act as heterogeneous nucleation sites for the L21 precipitates; The intragranular L21 precipitates contribute to the strengthening through the Orowan bowing mechanism. Mechanism: The shear band-driven precipitate dispersion leads to the formation of semicoherent nanoprecipitates, which enhances the strength and ductility of the alloy. Limitations: The limited process windows in conventional processing restrict the refinement of grains to sizes smaller than ~2 μm. Future work: Further investigation of the deformation mechanism and the effect of processing parameters on the microstructure and properties of the alloy. card: Paper card. Question: How does the yield and failure strength of a (Hf-Ta-Zr-Nb)C high-entropy carbide compare to its base monocarbides (HfC, TaC) during micropillar compression, and which slip systems operate under specific crystallographic orientations at room temperature?. System: (Hf-Ta-Zr-Nb)C high-entropy carbide, HfC monocarbide, TaC monocarbide. Processing: Ball-milling of equiatomic powders followed by spark-plasma sintering (SPS) with a two-step heating profile: 10 min dwell at 1800 °C and 7 min dwell at 2300 °C (Methods section states 2 min at 2300 °C, Abstract/Results state 7 min; text varies slightly but confirms SPS). Micropillars fabricated via FIB with diameter ~2.5 μm and height ~5 μm.. Test conditions: Room temperature micro-compression using an Agilent/Keysight G200 nanoindenter with a flat-punch diamond tip (5 μm diameter). Load-controlled mode, max load 100 mN, loading/unloading rate 0.02 mN/s. Grains selected with orientation Φ ~ 14° and φ2 ~ 45°.. Findings: The (Hf-Ta-Zr-Nb)C high-entropy carbide exhibited a yield strength of 6.20 ± 0.12 GPa, which is approximately 60% higher than the hardest base monocarbide HfC (3.93 ± 0.28 GPa).; TaC showed the lowest yield stress at 3.03 ± 0.11 GPa among the tested materials.; The high-entropy carbide demonstrated larger work hardening than HfC and similar ductility to TaC, with total deformation εHEC ~ 0.08 compared to εHfC ~ 0.06 and εTaC ~ 0.1.; Slip analysis confirmed the operation of {110}⟨11¯0⟩ slip systems in all three materials (HfC, TaC, and (Hf-Ta-Zr-Nb)C) at the specific orientation Φ ~ 14° and φ2 ~ 45°.; The calculated critical resolved shear stress (CRSS) for the {110}⟨11¯0⟩ system was 2.79 ± 0.05 GPa for the high-entropy carbide, 1.77 ± 0.13 GPa for HfC, and 1.36 ± 0.05 GPa for TaC.; Cracks initiated on the top surface of micropillars and propagated parallel to {001} facets, attributed to the pile-up of immobile a[001¯] dislocations formed by the interaction of {110} slip bands.. Mechanism: The authors propose that the enhanced strength is due to lattice distortion caused by the difference in atomic size and valence electron concentrations (VEC) of the transition metals, which hinders dislocation motion. The VEC of 8.5 in the high-entropy carbide increases the metallic character compared to HfC (VEC=8), improving ductility. The specific slip system ({110}⟨11¯0⟩) is determined by the crystal orientation and stress conditions (uniaxial compression) where the Schmid factor for {110} exceeds that of {111} for group IV-like behavior, despite TaC typically slipping on {111} under multiaxial indentation.. Limitations: The lattice structure of the high-entropy carbide has not been completely characterized. The study is confined to uniaxial stress conditions at a specific orientation, which may not represent the behavior under multiaxial stress fields like indentation. The quantitative comparison of micropillar results with theoretical simulations is noted as unreasonable due to differences in dislocation nucleation (homogeneous vs. heterogeneous).. Future work: Further DFT simulations are required to test the accuracy of predicting elastic properties for high-entropy carbides. The authors suggest that the dominant slip system during nanoindentation is likely {111}⟨11¯0⟩, differing from the {110} observed in compression, necessitating further investigation into the effect of different stress fields on slip activation.. Quote: "It was revealed that (Hf-Ta-Zr-Nb)C had a significantly enhanced yield and failure strength compared to the corresponding base monocarbides"

card: Paper card. Question: How can the Co-Ni balance in a VCrFeCoNi medium-entropy alloy system be tuned to induce an fcc to bcc martensitic transformation for enhancing cryogenic strength-ductility balance?. System: V10Cr10Fe45CoxNi35−x medium-entropy alloys (specifically 10Co, 20Co, 30Co, and 35Co variants). Processing: Vacuum induction melting of pure elements (99.9% purity), homogenization at 1100 °C for 6 hrs, cold-rolling with 75% reduction ratio to 1.5-mm sheets, and annealing at 900 °C for 10 min followed by water-quenching. Test conditions: Tensile testing at room temperature (25 °C) and cryogenic temperature (−196 °C) with a crosshead speed of 6.4 × 10−3 mm·s−1. Findings: The 35Co alloy achieved a cryogenic tensile strength of 1623 MPa, which is twice its room-temperature strength.; At cryogenic temperature, the 35Co alloy exhibited 65% elongation and a yield strength of 653 MPa.; The fraction of fcc phase in the 35Co alloy decreased to 1.1% after cryogenic tensile deformation, indicating extensive fcc to bcc transformation.; The 30Co alloy showed a multiple-stage strain hardening behavior with a hardening rate reaching 3600 MPa in Stage III.; The hcp phase fraction was approximately 5% and acted primarily as a nucleation site for the bcc martensite.; Increasing Co content from 10 to 35 at.% reduced the Gibbs free energy difference (ΔGbcc-fcc) from −1300 to −5800 J·mol−1.; The 35Co alloy displayed a sigmoidal stress-strain curve at cryogenic temperatures, consisting of an easy deformation stage followed by rapid hardening.. Mechanism: The fcc to bcc martensitic transformation generates a complex network structure with high-angle grain boundaries that refines the grain dynamically and introduces large transformation strains, creating mobile dislocations that significantly enhance strain hardening and strength-ductility balance.. Limitations: The authors note that thermodynamic calculations using the database are not accurate below 0 °C, though 0 °C calculations are considered reasonably acceptable for stability evaluation.. Future work: The authors propose that the fcc to bcc transformation can be an attractive route for a new MEA design strategy to improve cryogenic strength-ductility.. Quote: "The Co-Ni balance plays a leading role in phase stability and consequently tunes the cryogenic-temperature strength-ductility balance."

card: Paper card. Question: How can room-temperature deformation twinning be induced in a high-entropy alloy to improve cryogenic tensile properties, and can non-recrystallized grains be utilized to achieve ultra-high yield strength while maintaining ductility?. System: 10V15Cr5Mn35Fe10Co25Ni (at.%) high-entropy alloy. Processing: Vacuum induction melting followed by homogenization at 1,100 °C for 6 h; cold rolling at room temperature with a 75% reduction ratio to produce 1.5-mm-thick sheets; annealing at 750 °C for 10 min to obtain partially recrystallized microstructure (H750) or at 900 °C for 10 min for fully recrystallized microstructure (H900); water quenching.. Test conditions: Tensile testing at room temperature and cryogenic temperature (−196 °C) using a crosshead speed of 6.4 × 10−3 mm s−1.. Findings: The H750 alloy achieved a yield strength of 970 MPa and a tensile strength of 1,314 MPa at cryogenic temperatures.; The H750 alloy maintained a persistent elongation of 46.3% at cryogenic temperatures.; Non-recrystallized grains in the H750 alloy had an average size of ~32 μm, while recrystallized grains averaged ~1.5 μm.; Deformation twins with thicknesses of 10–30 nm were observed in recrystallized grains at cryogenic temperatures.; Primary twin bundles of ~500 nm thickness and secondary twins of 30–70 nm thickness formed in non-recrystallized grains at cryogenic temperatures.; The yield strength of the H750 alloy was ~270 MPa higher than that of the fully recrystallized H900 alloy at cryogenic temperatures.; Room-temperature cold rolling induced deformation twins in coarse grains without prior hot rolling, which were retained after partial recrystallization.. Mechanism: The critical stress for twinning decreases with increasing grain size, allowing twins to form readily in coarse non-recrystallized grains during cold rolling at room temperature. These retained twins act as strong barriers against mobile dislocations, enhancing yield strength. At cryogenic temperatures, additional deformation twins form in both recrystallized and non-recrystallized regions, leading to a high strain-hardening effect and ultra-high strength.. Limitations: The text does not explicitly state limitations of the study, though it notes that non-recrystallized regions are generally avoided in conventional alloys due to deleterious effects on ductility.. Future work: The authors propose that the combination of room-temperature deformation twinning and non-recrystallization offers a strengthening mechanism for ultra-high-strength HEAs and suggest the alloy is promising for applications in ultra-high-strength HEAs at cryogenic temperatures.. Quote: "Our results demonstrate that non-recrystallized grains, which are generally avoided in conventional alloys because of their deleterious effect on ductility, can be useful in achieving high-strength high-entropy alloys."

card: Paper card. Question: Is polymorphism still possible in entropy-stabilized high-entropy alloys (HEAs) that are generally believed to possess extremely high structural stability and maintain a single-phase structure?. System: Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy (Cantor's alloy). Processing: Synthesized via gas-atomization (melt injected into high purity Ar at 4 MPa pressure); subjected to hydrostatic compression up to ~41 GPa using a diamond anvil cell (DAC) with helium as pressure-transmitting medium; subsequently heated using resistive heating (up to 723 K) or double-sided Nd:YLF laser heating (up to ~1,400 K) at various pressures (6, 14, 26 GPa).. Test conditions: Room temperature compression up to ~41 GPa; heating at ambient pressure up to 723 K; heating at 6, 14, and 26 GPa up to ~1,400 K; in situ synchrotron radiation X-ray diffraction (XRD) monitoring.. Findings: The fcc-to-hcp polymorphic transition starts at approximately 22 GPa and almost completes at approximately 41 GPa.; The phase transition is irreversible; the hcp phase is retained when pressure is released to ambient conditions.; The hcp phase remains stable up to 633 K at ambient pressure before transforming back to fcc.; At 26 GPa, the critical temperature for the hcp-to-fcc transition is approximately 1,400 K.; The isothermal bulk modulus (B0) is 153.9±3.0 GPa for the fcc phase and 150.2±4.6 GPa for the hcp phase.; The c/a ratio of the hcp phase remained almost constant at 1.62±0.01 during compression and decompression.; The transition is sluggish, with fcc and hcp phases coexisting over a wide pressure range of ~22 to ~41 GPa.; Decompression from different maximum pressures yields fcc/hcp composites with tunable fractions.. Mechanism: The transition occurs because the hcp structure is thermodynamically more favorable at lower temperatures and high pressures, while the fcc phase is stable at higher temperatures and lower pressures; the transition is kinetically hindered by high energy barriers and low stacking fault energy (~20 mJ m−2), requiring high pressure to overcome these barriers to form the hcp phase.. Limitations: The transition is sluggish and irreversible, making it difficult to determine the real equilibrium phase boundary (Clapeyron coexistence curve) experimentally; grain size was not small enough for statistically reliable Rietveld refinement of volume fractions; overshooting often exists due to high energy barriers.. Future work: The authors suggest that this behavior could be general in various HEAs and propose new avenues for tailoring HEA properties via polymorphic transition-induced HEA composites, particularly at cryogenic temperatures where transition pressure could be largely decreased.. Quote: "The transition is irreversible, and our in situ high-temperature synchrotron radiation X-ray diffraction experiments at different pressures of the retained hcp high-entropy alloy reveal that the fcc phase is a stable polymorph at high temperatures, while the hcp structure is more thermodynamically favourable at lower temperatures."

card: Paper card. Question: How can bulk soft magnetic materials achieve a combination of high strength and good ductility without significantly deteriorating their soft magnetic properties (specifically coercivity)?. System: Non-equiatomic Fe35-x/3Co30-x/3Ni30-x/3Ta5Alx (x = 3, 5, 7 at%) high-entropy alloys, specifically the 7Al-HEA variant with a face-centered cubic matrix and L12 nanoprecipitates.. Processing: As-cast plates (10-mm thick) were hot-rolled at 1473 K to 50% thickness reduction, followed by 10-min homogenization at 1473 K and water quenching.. Test conditions: Tensile testing at room temperature; magnetic properties measured via vibrating sample magnetometry (VSM) and magneto-optical Kerr microscopy; microstructure analyzed via TEM, APT, and 4D-STEM.. Findings: The 7Al-HEA achieved an ultimate tensile strength of 1526 MPa with a tensile elongation of 15.3%.; The yield strength of the 7Al-HEA (1202 MPa) was approximately 245% higher than the base alloy (501 MPa).; The coercivity of the 7Al-HEA was 10.7 Oe, only marginally increased from 8.6 Oe in the 3Al-HEA.; The saturation magnetization (Ms) of the 7Al-HEA was 88 Am2 kg-1, compared to 105 Am2 kg-1 for the 3Al-HEA.; The L12 nanoprecipitates had an average size of 13.5 ± 2.5 nm and a volume fraction greater than 42% in the 7Al-HEA.; Dynamic microband refinement reduced the mean distance between parallel microbands from 735 ± 251 nm to 163 ± 35 nm as local strain increased from 30% to 50%.; The 7Al-HEA maintained 61% of its room temperature Ms value at 773 K.; The lattice strain at the coherent interface varied between -0.2% and 0.5% for the 7Al-HEA.. Mechanism: Strength is enhanced by massive solid solution strengthening, precipitation strengthening via shearing of coherent ordered L12 nanoprecipitates, and dynamic microband refinement. Soft magnetic properties are preserved because the full coherency between the nanoprecipitates and the matrix creates negligible distortion fields, resulting in insignificant pinning of Bloch domain walls compared to grain boundaries.. Limitations: The text does not explicitly state limitations of the study, though it notes that conventional strengthening approaches usually significantly deteriorate soft magnetic properties due to Bloch wall interactions with defects.. Future work: The findings provide guidance for developing new high-performance materials with an excellent combination of mechanical and soft magnetic properties as needed for the electrification of transport and industry.. Quote: "Compared to the alloy in precipitate‐free state, the alloy variant with a large volume fraction (>42%) of nanoprecipitates achieves significantly enhanced strength (≈1526 MPa) at good ductility (≈15%), while the coercivity is only marginally increased (<10.7 Oe)."
